title: Overfitting: reducing model capacity
prompt: A very large network gets 100% training accuracy and 46% validation accuracy. Which change most directly reduces its capacity to memorize training details?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Replace tanh with sigmoid
choices.explanation: Changes the activation but does not directly reduce the number of adjustable connections.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increase the hidden-layer width
choices.explanation: Usually adds capacity and more parameters.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reduce the number of hidden units
choices.explanation: Fewer hidden units usually mean fewer learned connections and less capacity.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Choose hyperparameters on the test set
choices.explanation: Leaks test information and does not itself simplify the model.

example: A student with a separate rule for every practice problem can memorize rather than learn. Reducing hidden units limits how many rules the network can express. For a bias-free 10→20→1 network, there are 220 weights; using 10→5→1 leaves 55. That is a direct capacity reduction, although validation must determine whether it helps.
takeaway: The question asks for direct capacity reduction. Smaller models can help overfitting but can also underfit.

title: CNN learned spatial feature extraction
prompt: Which operation learns local spatial patterns, such as edges, using trainable filters that are shared across image locations?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Convolution
choices.explanation: A learned kernel scans local neighborhoods and reuses its weights at different positions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Max pooling
choices.explanation: Selects local maxima without learning a filter.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sigmoid activation
choices.explanation: Applies a fixed elementwise function; it does not scan a learned spatial kernel.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Batch normalization
choices.explanation: Normalizes and applies scale/shift; it is not the learned spatial-filter operation.

example: Imagine a 2×2 patch [2,8;5,3] and a learned kernel [1,−1;0,0]. Their dot product is 2×1+8×(−1)+5×0+3×0=−6 before bias. The same kernel can slide to other patches. Unlike max pooling, the weights are adjustable and training can make the filter respond to useful patterns.
takeaway: Convolution learns shared local filters. Max pooling selects values. This wording asks about feature extraction, not minimum arithmetic cost.

title: All-zero initialization in a specified multilayer network
specificTopic: All-zero initialization in a specified multilayer network
prompt: A standard two-layer MLP uses h=tanh(W₁x), ŷ=W₂h, and squared loss. Both weight matrices start at zero, and gradients are computed before either matrix is updated. After this first update, what is W₁?

choices.label: A
choices.text: All entries positive
choices.explanation: No positive sign is forced; its gradient is zero.

choices.label: B
choices.text: All entries negative
choices.explanation: No negative sign is forced; its gradient is zero.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Necessarily a mix of positive and negative entries
choices.explanation: The downstream zero matrix prevents that first hidden-layer update.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Still all zeros
choices.explanation: The first hidden-layer gradient contains W₂ᵀ, which is zero.

takeaway: Zero downstream weights can block the first hidden-layer gradient. Compute all gradients using the pre-update parameters.

title: Parameters in multiple 1×1 filters

title: Gradient clipping versus vanishing gradients

choices.label: A

choices.explanation: That would normalize it upward, which the min prevents.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It becomes zero
choices.explanation: Clipping does not discard a gradient merely for being small.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It remains (0.03,0.04)
choices.explanation: Its norm is 0.05, so the scale is min(1,20)=1.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It shrinks by a factor of 20
choices.explanation: The gradient is below the threshold, so no shrinking is triggered.

takeaway: Clipping caps large gradients; it does not amplify small ones.

title: RNN vanishing-gradient diagnosis
prompt: An RNN runs without NaN or overflow, but early time steps receive gradients near zero. Along the backward path, most scalar derivative factors are around 0.5. What is the best explanation?

choices.explanation: Repeated factors below one shrink the backward signal.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Exploding gradients
choices.explanation: Explosion describes growing, not shrinking, gradient magnitudes.

title: Testing average-pooling linearity
prompt: Let f(x₁,x₂)=(x₁+x₂)/2 over a fixed pair of entries. Which statement is correct?

choices.explanation: Whether an operation learns weights does not determine linearity.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is linear because it satisfies additivity and homogeneity
choices.explanation: A fixed average is a linear combination of its inputs.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is equivalent to max pooling
choices.explanation: An average and a maximum generally give different outputs.

choices.label: D

choices.explanation: The average has no ReLU-style breakpoint.

takeaway: Average pooling is linear on a fixed window; max pooling is not.

title: Depth without nonlinear activations

choices.explanation: Composition does not multiply x by itself.

choices.label: B

choices.explanation: There is no nonlinearity to prevent affine collapse.

choices.explanation: The weights compose by multiplication, not addition.

choices.explanation: Substitution gives 2(3x+2)−1=6x+3.

title: Exploding chain-rule products
prompt: Along a scalar gradient path, each of ten local derivative factors is 2. Ignoring other branches, what happens to an upstream gradient of 1?

title: Conditional statements and unsupported conclusions
prompt: A hypothetical course announcement says, “A curve may be applied depending on the final score distribution.” Which conclusion is logically supported? This is a practice statement, not a claim about current course policy.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A curve is ruled out

choices.label: C
choices.text: A curve is possible but not guaranteed
choices.explanation: Matches the conditional nature of the announcement.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Every student must receive the same fixed increase
choices.explanation: No adjustment size or rule for individual students is supplied.

example: “We may change the plan if needed” leaves both outcomes open: the plan might change, or it might not.
